title: Behavioral Patterns Part 1
subtitle: Chain of Responsibility, Command, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Interpreter

scenes.title: Behavioral Patterns Part 1
scenes.subtitle: Chain of Responsibility, Command, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Interpreter

steps.say: Welcome to episode ten of the L-L-D Workshop, the low-level design series. Today: behavioral patterns, about how objects share work and talk.

By the end you'll be able to explain, draw and defend six of them: Chain of Responsibility, Command, Iterator, Mediator, Memento and Interpreter. Plus the classic bug for each, and how to tell look-alikes apart.
Keep the chapter ten PDF open beside the video. Every concept here matches a section there, with full Java code and real output. When a pause-and-think question appears, pause and answer before I do.

scenes.title: Behavioral patterns: the big picture

steps.say: Episode eight was about how objects are made. Episode nine was about how they're put together. Today's question is different: once the objects exist, who does what, and who calls whom?
Picture a restaurant kitchen. When an order arrives, who hears it first, who passes it on, and who can cancel it? That's behavior.

scenes.title: What behavioral patterns help you do
bullets: Let objects work together flexibly
Cut tight coupling between classes
Untangle many-object communication
Change behavior at run time, not only compile time

steps.say: Four goals. One: let objects cooperate flexibly. In our kitchen, a new station can join without retraining everyone.
Two: cut tight coupling. Coupling means one class depends heavily on another's internals. Less of it means each class is easier to change and to test.
Three: untangle communication, so ten objects calling each other gets a shape you can follow.
Four: change behavior at run time, like reordering checks from configuration, without recompiling.

scenes.title: The one idea behind all of them
scenes.caption: a chain of ifs, a hard-coded call, a loop... becomes an object

steps.say: Here's the single idea that runs through every behavioral pattern. Take behavior that's hidden inside a big method, like a chain of ifs, a hard-coded call or a loop, and turn it into an object.

Once it's an object you can name it, pass it around, swap it, store it and test it on its own. Keep that in mind; you'll see it six times today. Recap: behavioral patterns are about responsibility and communication.

scenes.title: The eleven GoF patterns: six today

head: Pattern
One-line intent
Ep
rows: Pass a request down a row of handlers
Wrap a request in an object
Walk a collection without seeing its storage
Private snapshot you can return to

steps.say: The Gang of Four book lists eleven behavioral patterns. Six today, five next time. Chain of Responsibility hands a request down a row of handlers.
Command wraps a request in an object.
Interpreter represents the grammar of a tiny language as classes, and evaluates sentences in it.
Iterator walks a collection one element at a time, without seeing how it's stored.
Mediator routes communication between many objects through one coordinator.
Memento lets an object privately snapshot its state and return to it.

scenes.title: The eleven GoF patterns: five next time

steps.say: Next episode: Observer, which notifies every dependent when something changes.
State, where an object's behavior changes with its internal state.
Strategy, which picks one of several interchangeable algorithms at run time.
Template Method, which fixes an algorithm's skeleton in a base class.
And Visitor, which adds operations without editing classes.

scenes.title: Which two behavioral patterns use inheritance?
bullets: A. Command and Memento
B. Template Method and Interpreter
C. Strategy and State
D. Iterator and Visitor

steps.say: Pause and think. Most behavioral patterns use composition, objects holding references to other objects. Only two share behavior through inheritance. Which two?

scenes.title: Class scope versus object scope

left.heading: Class scope: inheritance
bullets: Template Method, Interpreter
Fixed at compile time

right.heading: Object scope: composition
bullets: The other nine
Rewire objects at run time

steps.say: The answer is B. Template Method and Interpreter are class-scoped: subclasses inherit and fill in behavior.
That wiring is fixed when you compile.
The other nine are object-scoped. They use composition: objects hold references to other objects.
So you can rewire them while the program runs. Recap: eleven patterns, two by inheritance, nine by composition.

scenes.title: Chain of Responsibility

steps.say: You call a support line. Level one tries first. If they can't help, you go to level two, then to an engineer. But you only dialled one number. That's Chain of Responsibility, or C-o-R.

Definition: a request travels through a row of handler objects. Each one handles it, rejects it so nobody later sees it, or forwards it to the next. The sender only talks to the first handler and never learns who finished the job.

scenes.title: The problem: one method doing every check
bullets: Before creating an order: auth, rate limit, validation
The method grows with every new rule
The order of checks is hidden in the body
Some routes need only two checks: flags, copies

steps.say: Running example: an online shop's create-order A-P-I. A request must pass authentication, who is calling, rate limiting, are they calling too often, and validation, is the data well-formed.
Put it all in one method and problem one appears: every new rule makes it longer.
Problem two: the order of the checks is buried in the body, yet it matters. Auth then rate limit is a different system from rate limit then auth.
Problem three: some routes need only two of the checks. Soon you add boolean flags, then a second copy that somebody forgets to update.

scenes.title: How it works, step by step
bullets: 1. A Handler type: handle(request) + a next link
2. One concrete handler per check: stop or pass on
3. A terminal handler does the real work
4. Wire once at start-up
5. The client calls only the first handler

steps.say: Step one: an abstract Handler with a handle method and a reference to the next handler.
Step two: one small class per check. The Auth Handler checks the token. If it's missing, it returns false and the chain stops. Otherwise it passes the request on.
Step three: a terminal handler at the end does the real work. Here that's Create Order Handler, which never passes on.
Step four: wire it once at start-up: auth, set next rate limit, set next validate, set next create order.
Step five: the client calls only the first handler. Now the line is configuration, not logic. A new rule is one class plus one wiring line.

scenes.title: One chain, three different stopping points
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  C["Client"] --> A["Auth"]
  A -->|"ok"| R["Rate limit"]
  R -->|"ok"| V["Validate"]
  V -->|"ok"| O["Create order"]
  A -.->|"no token"| X1["Rejected"]
  R -.->|"over limit"| X2["Rejected"]
scenes.caption: each handler knows only the next one

steps.say: Here's the chain. A valid request flows all the way to Create Order.
A request with no token stops at Auth. The rate limiter, validator and order code never even run.
And a request over the limit stops at the rate limiter. Notice each handler knows only the next one, typed as the abstract Handler, so you can shuffle stages freely.

scenes.title: Walking four requests through the chain

head: Request
Path
Result
rows: auth ok, limit 1 of 2, valid, created

steps.say: Example time. Watch where each request stops.
Let's run it with a limit of two requests per user. Alice's first request: auth okay, rate limit one of two, valid, order created for two widgets.
Bob has no token. Auth rejects him, and nothing after auth runs.
Alice's second request has an empty body. It passes auth and the limiter at two of two, then validation rejects it.
Alice's third request is stopped by the limiter: three requests, limit two. Four requests, four different paths, one chain.

scenes.title: Order is a decision no tool verifies
bullets: Auth first: limiter can count per user
Auth first: anonymous floods can't burn a user's quota
Limit first: keys only on IP, but shields costly auth
Comment the reason beside the wiring

steps.say: Should auth come before rate limiting? Auth first means the limiter knows the user, so it counts per user.
It also means bad credentials are rejected before they use up a real user's quota.
Rate limiting first can only key on something like the I-P address. But it protects an expensive auth step from huge floods. Both are reasonable. They just behave differently.
No compiler checks this, so write the reason in a comment right next to the wiring. It's recorded nowhere else.

scenes.title: Bugs and variants to know

left.heading: Common bugs
bullets: Swallowing: neither handles nor passes on
No terminal handler: silent shrug
Shared stateful chain across requests

right.heading: Real-world chains
bullets: Servlet filters, Spring Security
Express next(), Go middleware
Logging levels, DOM event bubbling

steps.say: The classic bug is swallowing: a handler checks and just returns, without passing on. No error, and orders sometimes vanish. Give every path an explicit outcome, and test each handler against a fake next.
Second: no terminal handler. Falling off the end should throw, loudly.
Third: a filter chain keeps a position, so it's one per request, never shared.
Real chains: Java servlet filters and Spring Security.
Express middleware calls next. Passing next as an argument makes a forgotten call easy to spot.
And logging levels, where console, file and pager each act if severe enough. Strictly, if nobody can stop the flow, that's a pipeline.

scenes.title: In the interview, say this
scenes.caption: Decorator: all layers run.  Observer: everyone hears.  CoR: first taker wins

steps.say: Say: Chain of Responsibility splits a series of checks into handler objects, each linked only to the next. Only the wiring knows the order, so adding or reordering rules is cheap. Servlet filters are the everyday example. I give every path an explicit outcome and put a terminal handler at the end.

If they ask about Decorator: with Decorator every wrapper runs and the call always reaches the inside. With a chain, a handler can end the request. Recap: handle, reject, or pass on, and never swallow.

scenes.title: Command

steps.say: In a restaurant, the waiter writes an order slip and pins it on a rail. The cook acts on it later. The slip can be queued, prioritized or cancelled. The slip is a request turned into a thing. That's the Command pattern.

Definition: Command packages a request, like add two widgets to the cart, as an object holding everything needed to perform it later. Once it's an object, you can keep it, queue it, log it, retry it, and, if it knows its inverse, reverse it.

scenes.title: Why a plain method call isn't enough
bullets: Undo: reverse my last two changes
Queue: run later on a worker thread
Log of intent: what was requested
Retry with the same arguments
One action, many triggers: menu, hot-key, script

steps.say: Running example: a shopping cart. Calling cart dot set discount ten runs immediately and is forgotten. That fails five needs. One: undo, reverse my last two changes.
Two: a queue. Run the job later on a background worker thread, not the thread serving the user.
Three: a log of intent, recording what people asked for, not only the final state.
Four: retry a failed action with exactly the same arguments.
Five: one action, many triggers. A menu item, a keyboard shortcut and a script all fire the same apply-discount. Command gives the request a body that outlives the call.

scenes.title: The roles, in our cart

head: Role
Job
In our code
rows: State really changes; unaware of commands
Runs and remembers; unaware of carts

steps.say: Interviewers want three roles, invoker, command and receiver, plus the client. First, the Command interface, with execute and optionally undo.
A concrete command, like Add Item, stores its receiver, the cart, and its arguments: the S-K-U, meaning product code, and the quantity. It can do and undo exactly one operation.
The receiver is the Cart. Its state really changes, and it has no idea commands exist.
The invoker is Command History. It runs commands and remembers them, and it never mentions carts. So one history serves the whole app.
And the client, Main, builds a command and hands it its receiver.

scenes.title: Undo and redo, step by step
bullets: 1. Client builds command with receiver + args
2. Invoker executes; push on undo stack
3. Undo: pop, undo(), push on redo stack
4. Redo: pop redo, execute(), push back
5. A fresh command clears the redo stack

steps.say: Let's walk it with the cart. Step one: the client builds Add Item widget times two, and hands it to the history.
Step two: the history calls execute and pushes it on the undo stack, which is last-in, first-out. We run add widget two, add gadget one, then discount ten percent.
Step three, undo: pop the top, call its undo, push it on the redo stack. Undo twice: the discount goes, then the gadget goes.
Step four, redo: pop from redo, execute again, push back on undo. The gadget returns.
Step five: now we add three cables, a fresh command. The redo stack is cleared, so redo says nothing to redo.

scenes.title: Command flow
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  CL["Client"] -->|"builds"| CMD["AddItem widget x2"]
  CL -->|"hands to"| INV["CommandHistory"]
  INV -->|"execute"| CMD
  CMD -->|"cart.add"| REC["Cart"]
  INV --> U["Undo stack"]
  U <--> RD["Redo stack"]
scenes.caption: the invoker never knows what a command touches

steps.say: Here's the picture. The client builds a command and hands it to the invoker. The invoker calls execute, and the command calls the cart.
The invoker stacks it for undo, and moves it between the undo and redo stacks. Notice the command carries its own cart reference, because by the time it runs, its creator may be long gone.

scenes.title: Command: when it fits, when it doesn't

left.heading: Pros
bullets: Undo, queues, logs, retries become possible
One history for all commands
Macro command: commands of commands

right.heading: Skip it when
bullets: Simple, immediate call nobody undoes
A lambda already defers it
The effect can't truly be undone

steps.say: The wins: the request outlives the call, enabling undo, queues, logs and retries.
The invoker knows nothing about what it runs, so one history serves everything.
And a macro command, like a starter kit adding a keyboard, a mouse and fifteen percent off, runs steps in order and undoes them in reverse.
Skip it when the call is simple and immediate. A Save Command nobody undoes, queues or logs is extra code for nothing.
In Java, a Runnable already is a one-method command, and an Executor Service is its invoker. Write a class only for undo, a log name, or serialization.
And some effects can't be undone at all. That's our next concept.

scenes.title: Undo must restore, not recompute

steps.say: Here's a bug that looks harmless. The cart's undo for apply discount is written as: set the discount back to zero. What could go wrong?
Rule of thumb: execute must record whatever undo will need. Usually that's just the fields it overwrites, not a copy of the whole object.

scenes.title: The discount undo, guessed versus restored

steps.say: Example time. Same cart, two undo implementations.
Worked example. Our cart starts with a five percent discount, maybe a loyalty discount.
We execute Apply Discount ten percent. The correct version first saves the previous value, five, in a field called previous percent, then sets ten.

Now undo. The guessing version sets zero percent, a state the user never had. They just lost their loyalty discount. The restoring version sets five percent, exactly right. One field makes undo correct.

scenes.title: Two more undo rules
bullets: History is strictly last-in, first-out: a stack
Some effects escape: email sent, card charged
Honest options: keep out of history, or compensate
A refund is not an undo: both events stay recorded

steps.say: Rule two: undo history is strictly last-in, first-out. Add, add, discount is undone as discount, then the second add, then the first. Any other order can produce states that never existed.
Rule three: some effects escape your system, like a sent email or a charged card. An undo there promises the impossible.
So either keep them out of the history, like our Send Receipt command, or use compensation: a new action reaching a similar end state.
A refund for a charge is compensation. It's not an undo, because both the charge and the refund stay in the record. Recap: capture, then restore; use a stack; compensate what can't be undone.

scenes.title: Iterator

steps.say: Think of your T-V remote's next channel button. You have no idea how the channels are stored. You just press next. That's Iterator.

Definition: an iterator visits a collection's elements one at a time, in order, without knowing how they're stored: an array, a linked list, a tree, or a remote A-P-I that returns two results per page.

scenes.title: The problem it solves
bullets: Loops using get(i) assume an array
Many sources can't be indexed: trees, graphs, APIs
Every caller re-implements paging, some wrongly
Fix: a separate object with hasNext and next

steps.say: Running example: search results from a remote search A-P-I. Problem one: a loop that calls get i assumes an array. Move the data and every loop gets rewritten.
Problem two: many sources can't be indexed. A tree has several visiting orders. A graph has to remember visited nodes. A search A-P-I hands out pages.
So every caller writes its own paging code, and some get it wrong.
The fix: move the walking logic into a separate object that answers two questions. Has next: are there elements left? And next: give me the next one.

scenes.title: How it works, step by step
bullets: 1. Aggregate: iterator() returns a NEW iterator
2. Iterator: hasNext(), next()
3. The cursor lives inside the iterator
4. Client loops, or uses for-each

steps.say: Step one: the collection, which the Gang of Four calls the aggregate, has an iterator method that builds a brand-new iterator each time. In Java it implements Iterable. Our Paged Search Results does that.
Step two: the iterator implements has next and next. And next must throw No Such Element Exception when nothing is left. That's the contract.

Step three, the key detail: the current position, the cursor, lives inside the iterator, never in the collection. For paging, the cursor is the current page and an index into it. So two loops over the same data don't interfere.
Step four: the client writes while has next, use next. Or just a for-each loop, which the compiler turns into exactly that.

scenes.title: A plain loop over a paged API
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  L["for-each loop"] -->|"hasNext / next"| IT["PagedIterator"]
  IT -->|"buffer empty?"| API["Search API"]
  API -->|"2 results per page"| IT
  IT --> B["page buffer + index"]
scenes.caption: the loop never sees a page

steps.say: Here's the shape. The loop only calls has next and next.
When the buffered page runs out, has next calls the A-P-I for the next page. So has next is not a passive question. It can hit the network. Never assume it's cheap.

scenes.title: Example: five results, two per page

head: Loop step
What happens
rows: buffer empty: fetch page 1 -> result-1, result-2

steps.say: Example time. Watch the network calls.
Let's trace it. The A-P-I has five results, two per page. The first has next finds an empty buffer, so it fetches page one.
The loop sees result one and result two, straight from the buffer.
The buffer runs out, so has next fetches page two: results three and four.
Page three holds just result five.
And then has next fetches page four, which is empty. That's how it learns the data ended. Five items, four network calls. Remember that number.

scenes.title: Iterator variants and traps

left.heading: Kinds
bullets: External: client drives, can break early
Internal: forEach, streams drive
Tree iterator: a stack is the cursor

right.heading: Traps
bullets: Modify list mid-loop: exception, or skip
Reuse a one-shot iterator: empty
Early break leaks a file or DB cursor

steps.say: External iteration: the client drives, so it can stop early, like finding bob and breaking.
Internal iteration: the collection drives and calls your lambda, as in for each and streams.
A tree iterator keeps a stack of nodes still to visit. That stack is its position, so two iterators over one tree run independently.
Trap one: removing from an Array List inside a for-each usually throws. But remove the second-to-last element and the loop silently skips the last one. Use the iterator's remove, or remove if.
Trap two: a stream or Python generator is one-shot. Reuse it and you get nothing. That's why iterator must return a new object each time.
Trap three: a lazy iterator holding a file or database cursor leaks it if you break early. Use try-with-resources.

scenes.title: Why did five results take four network calls?
bullets: A. The iterator fetched page 1 twice
B. Without a total or next-page token, it must ask once more
C. hasNext always calls the API
D. The for-each loop retries

steps.say: Pause and think. The search A-P-I returned five results, two per page, yet we made four calls. Why?

scenes.title: Hide the shape, not the cost

steps.say: The answer is B. The A-P-I gave neither a total count nor a next-page token, so the only way to learn the data ended was to ask for one more page and get nothing back. That's real behavior, not a demo bug.

And here's the lesson. A tidy loop conceals the cost of each step. The famous N plus one query problem has exactly this shape: one query to load a list of orders, then one more query per order. A hundred orders, a hundred and one queries.

scenes.title: Keep the cost visible
bullets: Name the type honestly: PagedResults, not List
Offer a batch API with bigger pages
Return a total or a next-page cursor
Log or count fetches

steps.say: Four ways to keep the cost visible. One: name the type honestly. Call it Paged Results or Lazy Search Results, not List, so the reader expects network calls.
Two: offer a batch A-P-I. A caller who wants all ten thousand results can ask for pages of five hundred: twenty calls instead of five thousand.
Three: return the total, or a next-page cursor, when the source knows it. With a total of five, our loop stops after page three. Three calls, not four.

Four: log or count fetches, so a growing request count gets noticed in a dashboard. In the interview, say: iterators hide the shape of the data, but they shouldn't hide the cost. Recap: honest names, batches, totals, counters.

scenes.title: Java's iterator family

steps.say: Java gives you a whole family of iterator types. One row at a time.
Iterable: implementing it lets your class work in a for-each loop, like our Paged Search Results.
Iterator: has next, next, and an optional remove, the safe way to delete while looping.
List Iterator: goes both directions, and can set or add at the current spot.
Spliterator: an iterator that splits itself for parallel streams. For one to eight, try split hands off one to four and keeps five to eight; the parallel sum is thirty-six.
Enumeration: the old Java one point oh version. Use Iterator instead.

scenes.title: Fail-fast, weakly consistent, snapshot

head: Iterator kind
Example
On a change mid-loop
rows: Never throws; may or may not see it
Never throws; sees the old copy

steps.say: Three behaviors when the collection changes during a loop. Fail-fast: Array List and Hash Map detect a structural change and throw Concurrent Modification Exception. But the docs say best-effort, so never rely on it. And despite the name, it's usually one thread changing its own list inside its own loop.
Weakly consistent: Concurrent Hash Map's iterators never throw, and may or may not show changes made during the loop.

Snapshot: Copy On Write Array List iterates a frozen copy. In our demo, looping over x and y while adding x-bang and y-bang ends with four items, and the loop never saw the new ones. Recap: know which of the three you're holding.

scenes.title: Mediator

steps.say: Airplanes near an airport don't talk to each other. They all talk to the control tower, which holds the rules about spacing and order. That tower is a mediator.
Definition: Mediator makes a group of objects talk through one coordinator instead of referencing each other. Each object only reports this just happened. The mediator decides how the others respond.

scenes.title: The problem: four widgets that all know each other
bullets: Country picker -> refreshes delivery methods
Delivery method -> changes the price
Price -> decides if submit is clickable
Some countries: no delivery at all

steps.say: Running example: a checkout form with four widgets. Picking a country refreshes the list of delivery methods.
Choosing a delivery method changes the price label.
The price situation decides whether the submit button is clickable.
And some destinations, like Antarctica, have no delivery at all. If widgets call each other directly, each holds references to the other three, and none of them can be reused on another screen.

scenes.title: Links: everyone-to-everyone versus a hub
scenes.caption: 4 widgets: 6 links vs 4.   5 widgets: 10 links vs 5

steps.say: Let's count. If every widget knows every other, n widgets need n times n minus one, over two links. Four widgets: six links. Five widgets: ten. That grows roughly with the square.

With a mediator, each widget holds exactly one reference. Four widgets, four links. Add a promo code field and you get five, not ten. But here's the honest trade: the dependencies aren't removed. They're relocated into the mediator.

scenes.title: How it works, step by step
bullets: 1. Mediator interface: notify(sender, event)
2. Each component holds only the mediator
3. On an event: mediator.notify(this, event)
4. Concrete mediator holds the rules
5. It calls back down: two-way traffic

steps.say: Step one: a Mediator interface with one method, notify, taking the sender and the event.
Step two: each component, called a colleague, holds a reference to the mediator, and nothing else. Country Select doesn't know a price label exists.
Step three: when the user picks Germany, Country Select calls mediator dot notify, this, Germany. It reports up, and never calls a sibling.
Step four: the Shipping Form Mediator holds all the rules. When the country changes: reload methods, then show the price, then enable or disable submit.
Step five: it calls back down into specific widgets. Traffic is two-way through one object.

scenes.title: The shipping form hub
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart TB
  M["ShippingFormMediator"]
  C["CountrySelect"] -->|"notify"| M
  M -->|"setOptions"| D["MethodSelect"]
  D -->|"notify"| M
  M -->|"show"| P["PriceLabel"]
  M -->|"setEnabled"| S["SubmitButton"]
scenes.caption: widgets report up; the mediator instructs down

steps.say: Here's the hub. Widgets report upward with notify. The mediator instructs the widgets downward.
No arrow goes from one widget to another. That's the guarantee, and one shortcut reference in code review breaks it.

scenes.title: Example: one click updates three widgets

head: User action
Mediator does
rows: methods = standard, express; price 5.00; submit on
methods empty; no shipping; submit off

steps.say: Example time. Watch who calls whom.
Let's run it. The user picks Germany. The mediator reloads methods to standard and express, defaults to standard, shows five euros, and enables submit. Order matters: methods first, then price.
The user picks express. The method widget notifies, and the mediator shows fifteen.
Submit is clicked, and the mediator places the order: Germany, express.
Then Antarctica: no methods, price says shipping not available, submit disabled, and a click is ignored. One user action updated three widgets, and no widget called another.

scenes.title: Keep the mediator from becoming a god object

left.heading: Risks
bullets: Every new rule lands in the mediator
Merge conflicts in one shared file
It grows into a god object

right.heading: Defences
bullets: Split per screen area or workflow
Coordination only: no tax maths
Dispatch by table, not an if-chain

steps.say: The risks. Every new rule lands in the mediator, so it keeps growing.
Everyone editing the screen edits that one file, so merge conflicts pile up.
And it can become a god object, a class that knows and does too much.
Defence one: split it. One mediator per screen section or workflow. Two eighty-line mediators beat one with a hundred and sixty.
Defence two: keep it to coordination. Tax and pricing go in their own classes. The mediator decides what to call, not how to compute.

Defence three: dispatch with a map from event to handler, so each rule is easy to find. Real mediators: U-I view-models, chat servers, and saga orchestrators running payment, stock and shipping in order.

scenes.title: Mediator or Observer?

steps.say: This is a favourite interview question. Four differences, one row at a time.
Both patterns decouple objects. The difference is what happens to the news. With Mediator, the event travels together with a decision about what should follow. With Observer, only the event travels.
With Mediator, the reaction logic sits in one place. With Observer, it's spread across observers, each deciding alone.
Mediator traffic is two-way: colleagues report in, and the mediator calls out. Observer is one-way: the subject publishes, observers respond.
And order. A mediator writes the order explicitly. Observers should never depend on each other's order.

scenes.title: The practical test: does something need coordinating?

left.heading: Observer
bullets: Country changed: anyone interested, update
Listeners decide

right.heading: Mediator
bullets: Country changed: methods, then price, then submit
Hub decides and gives orders

steps.say: Apply it to our form. Country changed, anyone interested, update yourself. That's Observer, and it's lighter.
With Observer, the listeners decide.
But: country changed, so refresh methods, then price the new default, then decide submit. That's sequenced coordination. That's Mediator.

The hub decides and gives orders. In microservices, a central saga orchestrator is mediator style, and services reacting to each other's events is observer style. Recap: when the sequence matters, pick Mediator.

scenes.title: Memento

steps.say: In a video game you save your progress. The menu lists saves by name and date and loads one, but it never understands what's inside the save file. That's Memento.
Definition: Memento lets an object record its internal state in a snapshot and later return to it, while nobody else can see inside the snapshot.

scenes.title: The problem: rollback without breaking privacy
bullets: Snapshot a deployment config before a risky rollout
Outside class reading every field breaks encapsulation
Field-by-field restore can stop half-way
Fix: the object snapshots itself into a sealed token

steps.say: Running example: a deployment config with replicas, meaning how many copies run, an image, meaning which build, and environment variables, meaning named settings. Before a risky release we save it.
If an outside history class reads and stores every field, encapsulation breaks. Every new config field changes the history class, and private details leak.
And atomicity breaks, meaning all-or-nothing. A field-by-field restore can write three fields, hit an exception, and leave a combination that never existed.
The fix: the object takes its own snapshot, and hands out a sealed token only it can open. Restore is one call into the object.

scenes.title: The three roles

head: Role
Job
In our code
rows: Carries the state; opaque to others

steps.say: Three roles. The originator owns the state, and produces and consumes snapshots: Deployment Config.

The memento carries the state. To everyone else it's opaque. In Java, the public Snapshot interface exposes only a label. The data sits in a private nested record called State, which only Deployment Config can see.
The caretaker, Deployment History, decides when to save and restore, and never looks inside. Quick check: if the caretaker names the config fields, it's not really a memento.

scenes.title: Example: checkpoint, bad rollout, rollback

head: Step
Live config
rows: snapshot sealed and pushed on a stack
replicas 10, image api 2.0, debug, FEATURE_X on

steps.say: Example time. A real rollback, step by step.
Let's run it. We start with three replicas, image A-P-I version one point four, log level info.
The caretaker takes a checkpoint named before two point oh. The config hands back a sealed snapshot, and history pushes it on a stack.
The rollout changes everything: ten replicas, version two point oh, debug logging, and a feature flag turned on in the live map.

Rollback: history pops the snapshot and calls restore. The config checks the token is really one of its own, then assigns every field in one step. We're back to three replicas, version one point four, info. And if someone forges a snapshot, restore refuses it.

scenes.title: The snapshot bug: aliasing mutable state

steps.say: Notice in that rollback, we changed the live environment map after saving, and the rollback still worked. That's not automatic. It's the most common Memento bug.
If the snapshot holds a pointer to the very same map the object keeps changing, it's not a snapshot. That's called aliasing: two names for one mutable object.

scenes.title: Bad snapshot versus good snapshot

left.heading: Bad: shares the live map
bullets: snapshot = liveEnv
live set to debug: snapshot shows debug

right.heading: Good: owns a copy
bullets: snapshot = copy of liveEnv
live set to debug: snapshot still info

steps.say: Worked example. The live map says log level info. The bad snapshot just points at the live map.
Now we change live to debug. The bad snapshot also says debug, because it is the same map. Restore re-applies today's state. Nothing throws, until someone notices the rollback did nothing.
The good snapshot copies the map. In our code, the State record's constructor does Map dot copy of.
So when live changes to debug, the good snapshot still says info.

scenes.title: Rules that keep snapshots honest
bullets: Copy every mutable part: Map.copyOf, deep copies
Same shallow-versus-deep choice as Prototype
Bound the history: drop the oldest
Don't snapshot sockets, open files, other systems

steps.say: Rule one: copy every mutable part. Map dot copy of, or a deep copy, meaning you duplicate the objects inside too.
This is the same shallow-versus-deep decision you met with Prototype in episode eight.
Rule two: bound the history. Ours holds two checkpoints, so saving a third drops the oldest. Kubernetes keeps ten revisions by default. An endless list is a memory leak.

Rule three: some state can't be captured: live network connections, open files, data owned by another system. A snapshot claiming to cover those fails, usually long after the mistake. Recap: copy, bound, and only snapshot what you can restore.

scenes.title: Memento versus Command undo

steps.say: Here's a classic comparison. Five rows.
Two ways to build undo. What's saved per step? Memento saves a full copy of the state. Command saves the operation plus the little bit of state its reversal needs.
How does undo happen? Memento re-installs an earlier copy. Command runs the opposite operation.
Memory: Memento grows with the size of the state. Command grows with the size of one operation.
Correctness: Memento is low risk, because the copy was a real state. With Command, every inverse must be written correctly.
So prefer Memento when reversal is tricky or the state is small. Prefer Command when reversal is simple or the state is big.

scenes.title: Two examples, then the combination
bullets: Drawing app: canvas per stroke runs out of memory
so use Command: stroke added, here are its points
Wizard step changes six linked fields
so use Memento: one snapshot beats six inverses
Real systems: periodic snapshots + replay commands

steps.say: Example one: a drawing app. Say the canvas is eight megabytes. Snapshot it on every brush stroke, and a thousand strokes cost eight gigabytes.
So use Command. Each step stores stroke added, here are its points. A few kilobytes.
Example two: a multi-step form wizard. Step three changes six fields that interact.
Writing six correct inverse operations is risky. One small snapshot is simpler and always correct. Memento wins.

Real systems combine them. Take a snapshot every hundred edits, and log commands in between. To go back, restore the nearest snapshot and replay forward. Databases and event-sourced systems do exactly this. Recap: Memento stores state, Command stores actions; pick whichever is smaller.

scenes.title: Interpreter

steps.say: A calculator reads two plus three times four. It knows times binds tighter, builds two plus three-times-four, and works from the inside out. That's Interpreter.

Definition: Interpreter represents the grammar of a small language as classes, one class per grammar rule. It evaluates a sentence by building a tree of those objects and asking the root to interpret itself.

scenes.title: The vocabulary
bullets: Grammar: rules for valid sentences
DSL: a small language for one job
AST: the sentence as a tree
Terminal: a leaf, a number or variable
Nonterminal: built from other expressions
Context: outside info, like variable values

steps.say: Six words to know. Grammar: the rules for valid sentences. For example, an expression is terms joined by plus or minus.
D-S-L, a domain-specific language: a small language for one job, like pricing rules, search filters or feature-flag conditions.
A-S-T, an abstract syntax tree: the sentence as a tree, operators inside, numbers and variables at the leaves.
A terminal expression is a leaf rule: a number, or a variable.
A nonterminal expression is built from others: addition, multiplication.
And the context is outside information, like price is two hundred fifty. Why bother? Hard-coded rules need a redeploy each; a tiny language turns rules into data.

scenes.title: How it works, step by step
bullets: 1. Write the grammar: expr, term, factor
2. One class per rule: Constant, Variable, Binary
3. Parse text into an AST (not part of the pattern)
4. Interpret: root asks children, combines
5. Parse once, interpret many times

steps.say: Running example: price times qty minus discount. Step one, the grammar: an expr is terms joined by plus or minus, a term is factors joined by times or divide, and a factor is a number, a name, or brackets.
Step two: one class per rule. Constant and Variable are terminals. Negate and Binary are nonterminals. All implement interpret, taking a context.
Step three: build the tree. The Gang of Four deliberately leave parsing out of the pattern. Ours is recursive descent: one method per grammar rule, calling the others.
Step four: interpret. The root asks its children for their values and combines them, recursively.
Step five: reuse the tree. Parse once, interpret many times with different contexts.

scenes.title: The AST for price * qty - discount
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  M["Binary minus"] --> T["Binary times"]
  M --> D["Variable discount"]
  T --> P["Variable price"]
  T --> Q["Variable qty"]
scenes.caption: leaves and inner nodes share one interface: it's Composite + interpret

steps.say: Here's the tree. Minus is the root. Its left child is times, with price and qty under it. Its right child is discount.
Leaves and inner nodes share one interface, so this is the Composite pattern from episode nine. Interpreter is basically Composite plus an interpret operation.

scenes.title: Example: evaluating with a context

steps.say: Example time. One tree, many answers.
Context: price two hundred fifty, qty three, discount fifty. Times first: seven hundred fifty. Minus fifty: seven hundred.
Two plus three times four is fourteen. Why? The grammar handles times in term, one level below expr, so it binds tighter.
With brackets, two plus three, times four, is twenty.
Now reuse the same parsed tree. Quantity one gives two hundred, two gives four hundred fifty, four gives nine hundred fifty. No re-parsing.
And good errors: price times tax says unknown variable tax. Bad syntax reports the position. One note: real money rules should use Big Decimal, not double.

scenes.title: When to use it, when not

left.heading: Good fit
bullets: Tiny DSLs: promotions, filters, flags
Regex Pattern, SpEL, cron expressions

right.heading: Use something else
bullets: Big grammar: ANTLR parser generator
Many operations on the tree: Visitor
Users and scripts: keep the DSL small

steps.say: Good fit: tiny D-S-Ls, like ten percent off if the cart is over nine ninety-nine and category is electronics.
Real examples: Java's regex Pattern builds a node tree that a Matcher walks, and Spring's expression language does the same.
Not a fit: a big grammar like S-Q-L. Use a parser generator such as ANTLR, which writes a parser from a grammar file.
And when operations on the tree multiply, like type-check and pretty-print, move to Visitor, next episode.

Security: never let users run a general-purpose script engine on your server. A small, restricted language is safer because it can only do what its grammar allows. Recap: one class per rule, parse once, interpret with a context.

scenes.title: The six patterns side by side

head: Pattern
Object you create
Often confused with
rows: Visitor: what to do at each node

steps.say: Here's the whole chapter on one slide.
Chain of Responsibility: a handler per check. Don't confuse it with Decorator, where every layer runs.
Command: an object per request. Versus Strategy: Strategy is how a job is done, Command is which job.
Iterator: a cursor object. Versus Visitor: Iterator decides how you move, Visitor decides what you do at each element.
Mediator: one coordinator. Versus Observer, which only broadcasts. And versus Facade, which sits in front of a subsystem, one-way.
Memento: a sealed snapshot. Versus Command undo, and versus Prototype, whose clone becomes a live object you keep using.
Interpreter: a node per grammar rule. It's built on Composite, and it moves to Visitor when operations multiply.

scenes.title: Combo facts and a final quiz
bullets: The request in a chain is often a Command
A Mediator often creates and dispatches Commands
Memento + Command: snapshots + replay
Interpreter = Composite + evaluate
Five dependent form widgets? Mediator
Business users write discount rules? Interpreter

steps.say: Interview combos. The request moving through a chain is often a Command, like a job checked by validation and authorization before a worker runs it.
A mediator often creates and dispatches commands.
Memento plus Command gives scalable undo: snapshots plus replay.
Iterator plus Composite walks trees, and Interpreter is Composite plus evaluate.
Quick quiz. Five form widgets depend on each other's values. Which pattern? Mediator.
Business users need to write their own discount rules. Interpreter, a small D-S-L. And undo for a text editor? Command per edit, with Memento snapshots now and then.

scenes.title: TL;DR: hidden control flow becomes named objects
bullets: Behavior: hidden control flow -> named objects
CoR: handle / reject / pass on; terminal handler
Command: restore captured state; stack; compensate
Iterator: cursor in iterator; keep cost visible
Mediator: small hub. Memento: copy, bound
Interpreter: rule = class. Next: Ep 11

steps.say: Behavioral patterns turn hidden control flow into named objects.
Chain of Responsibility: handle, reject or pass on. Order matters, always have a terminal handler, and never swallow a request.
Command: the request becomes an object. Undo restores captured state, history is a stack, and irreversible actions get compensation.
Iterator: the position lives in the iterator. Implement Iterable, know fail-fast versus snapshot, and don't let a lazy loop hide its cost.
Mediator: one hub, links grow linearly, but keep it small. Memento: the object snapshots itself, deep-copy mutable parts, bound the history.

Interpreter: one class per grammar rule, parse once, interpret with a context. Use each one when the flexibility is real. Next time, episode eleven: Observer, State, Strategy, Template Method and Visitor. See you there.
